title: Errors, Debugging & Testing
sub: Handle failures on purpose, read any traceback, step through code with pdb and PyCharm, and prove your functions work with tests
goals: Read a traceback from the bottom up and name the frame that holds the bug
Catch, raise, chain and define exceptions with try, except, else, finally and raise from
Choose between EAFP and LBYL and validate network data without crashing on the first bad line
Replace debugging prints with logging, breakpoint() and pdb commands
Debug in PyCharm with breakpoints, conditions, stepping, watches and Evaluate Expression
Write unittest and pytest tests and drive a function with a test-first loop

blocks.text: Every program you have written so far assumed that the input is well formed, the file exists and the host answers. Real data does not cooperate: a log line is cut off, a port number is `http`, a DNS server stays silent. This chapter teaches you what Python does at the moment something goes wrong, how to read the report it prints, how to decide which failures to handle and which to let through, and how to find the cause of a failure you do not understand yet. You will finish with a small, tested parser for ping output.

Create `~/lab/errors/` and open it as a PyCharm project (or just use `nano`). Many examples below are meant to be crashed on purpose. Type them, read what Python tells you, then fix them. The in-page blocks marked `raises` end with an exception deliberately; the red text under them is the lesson.
What an exception is

An **exception** is an object that Python creates when an operation cannot continue. It records what went wrong (its type and message) and where (a trace of the active function calls). **Raising** it interrupts normal execution: Python stops the current statement and starts **unwinding**, which means leaving the current function, then its caller, then the caller's caller, looking at each level for a matching `except` clause. If one is found, execution resumes there. If the unwinding reaches the top of the program, Python prints the traceback and exits with status 1.

blocks.code:
main()                    calls ──▶ load_targets()   calls ──▶ parse_target()   calls ──▶ str.split / int
    │                                    │                           │                          │
    │                                    │                           │                          ✖ ⟪r:ValueError raised here⟫
    │                                    │                           ◀── no handler: frame discarded
    │                                    ◀── no handler: frame discarded
    ◀── ⟪g:try / except ValueError⟫  handler found: execution resumes here

blocks.text: Nothing is lost on the way up. The exception object carries a **traceback** (a linked list of the frames it passed through), so the handler, or the final error report, can still say where it started.

blocks.out:
port 22
port 443
skipping 'http' -> invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'http'
port 8080
program continues

blocks.text: Without the `try`, the loop would have ended at `"http"` and `"8080"` would never be read. With it, the failure is confined to one item.

C functions often return `-1` and leave the real reason in a global variable; a caller that forgets to check carries on with garbage. An exception cannot be ignored by accident: if nobody handles it, the program stops loudly. The cost is that the handler may sit far from the failing line, which is why reading tracebacks (next section) is a core skill.
Reading a traceback

A traceback lists the calls that were active when the exception was raised, **oldest first, newest last**. The line you want to read first is the **last** one: it holds the exception type and message. The frame just above it is where the error surfaced. Save this program as `probe.py`; the third entry has no port, which will break it:

blocks.code:
$ python3 probe.py
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/Users/you/lab/errors/probe.py", line 19, in <module>
    print(load_targets(SERVICES))
          ~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/Users/you/lab/errors/probe.py", line 13, in load_targets
    name, host, port = parse_target(entry)
                       ~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^
  File "/Users/you/lab/errors/probe.py", line 6, in parse_target
    host, port = address.split(":")
    ^^^^^^^^^^
ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 2, got 1)

blocks.text: Read it in this order:

items.text: **Last line.** `ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 2, got 1)`. Something was split into one piece where two were needed.
**The frame directly above it.** `parse_target`, line 6, the statement `host, port = address.split(":")`. This is where Python gave up.

**The frames above that**, oldest at the top. `load_targets` called `parse_target` with some `entry`; `<module>` called `load_targets`. These tell you *which input* led here. The traceback does not print variable values, so you add them: a `print(repr(entry))` before line 13, or a breakpoint (later in this chapter).

**The markers.** Since Python 3.11 the `~~~^^^` carets underline the exact sub-expression being executed. Python 3.13 also colors the output in a terminal; set `NO_COLOR=1` to turn that off when you paste traces into a bug report.

blocks.text: The cause is the data (`"cache=192.0.2.30"` has no colon), the symptom is on line 6. The fix may belong in `parse_target` (validate and raise a clear error), in `load_targets` (skip and report bad entries) or in the data. Deciding that is the real work; the traceback only tells you where to start looking.

blocks.text: Chained exceptions
If a new exception is raised while another is being handled, Python prints both and joins them with a sentence that tells you how they relate. Run this `chain.py`:

blocks.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "chain.py", line 3, in read_port
    return int(text)
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'http'

During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "chain.py", line 8, in <module>
    print(read_port("http"))
          ~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^
  File "chain.py", line 5, in read_port
    raise RuntimeError("bad port in config")
RuntimeError: bad port in config

blocks.text: "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred" means the second error happened *accidentally or without saying why*. The explicit form, `raise ... from err`, prints "The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception" instead. Both show the root cause first, so scroll to the **top** chain entry when the final message looks too vague. The section on raising covers how to choose.

blocks.title: The error is often not on the line shown

blocks.text: Python reports where the problem was *detected*. A `None` returned three functions ago is detected when you call `.split()` on it. When the last frame looks innocent, walk up the frames and ask which value was already wrong when it arrived.
The common exceptions, one at a time
Nine exceptions account for most of the errors you will meet at this stage. Each block below ends with the exception on purpose, so press Run and read the red text.
**TypeError**: the operation does not apply to that type.

blocks.code:
port = 80
print("port " + port)

blocks.text: **ValueError**: the type is right, the value is not.

blocks.code: print(int("80/tcp"))

blocks.text: **KeyError**: a dict key that does not exist.

blocks.code:
host = {"ip": "192.0.2.1"}
print(host["port"])

blocks.text: **IndexError**: a list position that does not exist.

blocks.code:
ports = [22, 80, 443]
print(ports[3])

blocks.text: **ZeroDivisionError**: dividing by zero, including `%` and `//`.

blocks.code:
packets_sent = 0
print(100 * 3 / packets_sent)

blocks.text: **AttributeError**: the object has no such attribute or method.

blocks.code:
line = "64 bytes from 192.0.2.1"
line.push("x")

blocks.text: **NameError**: a name that is not defined in any visible scope, usually a typo or a use before assignment.

blocks.code:
total = 5
print(totl)

blocks.text: **ModuleNotFoundError** (a subclass of **ImportError**): the module is not installed or the name is misspelled.

blocks.code: import requestz

blocks.text: **FileNotFoundError** (a subclass of **OSError**): the path does not exist. The message includes an `errno` number; it differs between operating systems, so the number you see in this page is not the number you will see on your Mac.

blocks.code:
with open("/no/such/file.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())

blocks.text: The messages matter. This block collects them into a table by catching each one and printing its type and text, which is also how you would log them:

blocks.code:
def show(fn):
    try:
        fn()
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"{type(e).__name__:<20} {e}")

show(lambda: "port " + 80)
show(lambda: int("80/tcp"))
show(lambda: {"ip": "192.0.2.1"}["port"])
show(lambda: [22, 80, 443][3])
show(lambda: 100 / 0)
show(lambda: "64 bytes".push)
show(lambda: totl)
show(lambda: __import__("requestz"))
show(lambda: int(None))
blocks.out:
TypeError            can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
ValueError           invalid literal for int() with base 10: '80/tcp'
KeyError             'port'
IndexError           list index out of range
ZeroDivisionError    division by zero
AttributeError       'str' object has no attribute 'push'
NameError            name 'totl' is not defined
ModuleNotFoundError  No module named 'requestz'
TypeError            int() argument must be a string, a bytes-like object or a real number, not 'NoneType'

blocks.text: Notice how `KeyError` shows only the missing key with quotes, and that `int(None)` is a `TypeError` (wrong type) while `int("x")` is a `ValueError` (right type, wrong content). That distinction is how you decide which one to catch: `TypeError` is nearly always a bug in your code, `ValueError` is often bad input.
The hierarchy
Exceptions are classes arranged in an inheritance tree. An `except` clause for a class also catches all its subclasses.

blocks.code:
BaseException
   ├── SystemExit               raised by sys.exit()
   ├── KeyboardInterrupt        Ctrl+C
   ├── GeneratorExit
   └── Exception                ⟪g:everything you normally catch⟫
        ├── ArithmeticError
        │    ├── ZeroDivisionError
        │    └── OverflowError
        ├── LookupError
        │    ├── KeyError
        │    └── IndexError
        ├── ValueError
        │    └── UnicodeError  (UnicodeDecodeError, UnicodeEncodeError)
        ├── TypeError
        ├── AttributeError
        ├── NameError
        ├── ImportError
        │    └── ModuleNotFoundError
        ├── OSError                  (alias: IOError, EnvironmentError)
        │    ├── FileNotFoundError
        │    ├── PermissionError
        │    ├── ConnectionError
        │    │    ├── ConnectionRefusedError
        │    │    └── ConnectionResetError
        │    ├── TimeoutError
        │    └── BlockingIOError ...
        ├── RuntimeError
        │    └── RecursionError
        ├── AssertionError
        └── StopIteration

blocks.text: Two practical consequences. `except LookupError` handles both `KeyError` and `IndexError`. `except OSError` handles every file and network failure, and you can narrow it: `except ConnectionRefusedError` is "the host is up and nothing listens on that port", which a port scanner treats as a result and not as a failure.

blocks.code:
print(issubclass(KeyError, LookupError), issubclass(ZeroDivisionError, ArithmeticError))
print(issubclass(FileNotFoundError, OSError), issubclass(KeyboardInterrupt, Exception))
print([cls.__name__ for cls in ModuleNotFoundError.__mro__])

blocks.text: `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit` sit *outside* `Exception` on purpose, so that `except Exception` does not swallow Ctrl+C or `sys.exit()`.
try, except, else, finally

tokens.exp: begin a block whose exceptions you want to handle
the code that may raise; keep it as small as possible
run when a ValueError (or subclass) escapes the try block; err is the exception object
the recovery: log, substitute a default, or skip
run only when the try block finished with no exception
code that should not be protected by the except clauses above
always run last, whether the block ended normally, with an exception, or through return

blocks.code:
┌──────────────┐
               │  try: block  │
               └──────┬───────┘
          no error ┌──┴──┐ error raised
                   ▼     ▼
        ┌────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────┐
        │   else:    │  │ first matching      │──▶ no match: exception keeps travelling up
        │ (optional) │  │ except: clause runs │
        └─────┬──────┘  └──────────┬──────────┘
              └──────────┬─────────┘
                         ▼
                 ┌───────────────┐
                 │   finally:    │  ⟪y:always runs, even on return or a re-raised error⟫
                 └───────────────┘

blocks.text: Rules that follow from the mechanism:

items.text: **Clauses are tried top to bottom and the first match wins.** Put specific classes before general ones. `except Exception` first would shadow everything below it.

**`except (A, B) as err:`** with a tuple catches either. Without the parentheses the comma form is a `SyntaxError` before Python 3.14; from 3.14 `except A, B:` is allowed, but only without `as`, so keep the parentheses.
**`as err` is deleted when the clause ends.** Python removes the name to avoid a reference cycle between the exception and its traceback. Copy it (`saved = err`) if you need it later.
**Keep the `try` block small.** Everything inside it is protected, which means a bug in an unrelated line can be hidden by your handler.
**`else` is for the code that depends on success.** It is not protected by the `except` clauses, so errors in it propagate instead of being mistaken for the failure you expected.

blocks.out:
checked '443'
443
  'http' is not a number
  checked 'http'
None
  None is not text
  checked None
None
  70000 is out of range
  checked '70000'
None

blocks.text: Look at the order of the output. `finally` runs after the `return` statements have *decided* the return value but before the function actually returns, so "checked" prints before each result.

items.text: **Bare `except:`** also catches `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`, so Ctrl+C stops working. Write `except Exception:` at the broadest, and prefer a specific class.
**Silent `except Exception: pass`** converts every bug into "nothing happened". If you must ignore something, name the exact exception, and log it.
**`return` inside `finally`** replaces any exception in flight, discarding the error without a trace. Python 3.14 makes the compiler warn about it. Never do this.

blocks.text: The `ValueError` vanished. This is why `finally` is for cleanup only.

blocks.name: try
blocks.sum: Run a block and divert execution to a handler if it raises.
blocks.syntax: try: ... except Class as name: ... else: ... finally: ...

how.text: `try` marks a region. If any statement inside raises, Python abandons the rest of the block, walks the `except` clauses from top to bottom and runs the first whose class matches (the raised class or one of its parents). `else` runs only if nothing was raised. `finally` always runs once, last. At least one `except` or a `finally` is required.

The cost of a `try` block is close to zero when nothing is raised. Raising and catching costs more than an `if` check, which is fine for rare events and a reason not to use exceptions for ordinary control flow in a hot loop.

gotchas: The names after `except` are looked up when an exception happens, so a typo in an `except` clause is only found when that path runs.

blocks.name: except
blocks.sum: Select which exceptions a try block handles.
blocks.syntax: except Class: | except (A, B) as name: | except* Class:

how.text: `except` takes a class, a tuple of classes, or nothing (bare, which you should avoid). Matching uses `isinstance`, so a parent class matches its children. Inside the clause `name` is the exception object: `str(name)` gives the message, `name.args` the raw arguments, `type(name).__name__` the class name, `name.__traceback__` the frames. `except*` (Python 3.11+) handles `ExceptionGroup`s raised by concurrent code and is not needed for this book.

IndexError list index out of range
KeyError 'db'

examples.desc: Show which exception class a one-liner raises, for a quick lookup

gotchas: Catching `Exception` and printing only `str(e)` loses the type. A bare `KeyError('port')` prints as `'port'`. Log `repr(e)` or `type(e).__name__` too.

blocks.name: finally
blocks.sum: Run cleanup code whether or not the try block raised.

how.text: The `finally` clause runs when control leaves the `try` statement by any route: normal completion, an exception (handled or not), `return`, `break` or `continue`. If an exception is in flight it resumes after `finally` finishes. Prefer `with` for resources that support it, since it packages the same guarantee.

examples.desc: Cleanup runs even when the work fails
examples.out:
working
cleanup
caller saw the error

examples.desc: Remove a temp file whatever happens to the job
examples.code:
python3 -c 'import os, tempfile
fd, path = tempfile.mkstemp()
try:
    os.write(fd, b"scratch")
finally:
    os.close(fd); os.remove(path); print("removed")'

gotchas: Do not `return`, `break` or `continue` inside `finally`: it swallows the in-flight exception.

blocks.text: Raising your own exceptions
Your functions should **fail loudly and specifically** when asked to do something impossible. `raise` takes an exception instance (or class, which Python instantiates with no arguments):

blocks.out:
0xffffff00
ValueError: prefix must be 0..32, got 33
TypeError: prefix must be int, got str

blocks.text: Choose the class by the rule from the previous section: `TypeError` when the argument is the wrong kind of thing, `ValueError` when the kind is right and the content is not. The message should contain the offending value in `repr` form (`!r`), because the reader cannot see your variables.
Re-raising and chaining
Inside an `except` clause, a bare `raise` re-raises the current exception unchanged, keeping its original traceback. Use it to do something (log, count, clean up) and still let the caller decide.

`raise NewError(...) from err` **chains** two exceptions on purpose: the new exception explains the situation in your layer's vocabulary, and `__cause__` keeps the original so the traceback shows both. `from None` suppresses the context when the original adds only noise.

blocks.out:
error: port setting 'http' is not a number
cause: ValueError("invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'http'")

blocks.text: Since Python 3.11 you can also attach a note without changing the message: `err.add_note("while reading hosts.txt line 3")`. Notes print under the traceback and are the neat way to add context while re-raising.

blocks.out:
invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'x'
['while reading line 3 of hosts.txt']

blocks.text: Custom exception classes

Subclass `Exception` (never `BaseException`) to give callers something precise to catch. A small hierarchy with one base class lets a caller catch "anything from my library" with one clause and still distinguish the cases:

blocks.out:
ok 192.0.2.7
BadAddress | '192.0.2': not an IPv4 address
BadAddress | '192.0.2.256': not an IPv4 address
True
192.0.2.9 22 192.0.2.9:22 did not answer within 2.5s

blocks.text: `BadAddress` inherits from both `NetkitError` and the built-in `ValueError`, so code that already catches `ValueError` keeps working with your more specific error. Put the extra data (`host`, `port`) in attributes, not only in the message, so handlers can use it without parsing text.

blocks.name: raise
blocks.sum: Raise an exception, re-raise the current one, or chain two exceptions.

how.text: `raise Exc(...)` creates the exception object and starts unwinding. A bare `raise` inside an `except` clause re-raises the exception being handled with its traceback intact. `raise Exc(...) from err` sets `__cause__` and prints "the direct cause of the following exception"; `from None` hides the implicit context. The original traceback is attached to the exception as it propagates, so raising a *new* exception inside a handler always starts a fresh chain.

gotchas: `raise ValueError` (class, no parentheses) works but gives an empty message. Always include one.

blocks.text: Cleanup that cannot be forgotten: with, suppress

You met `with` in [Python files](#py-files): it calls `__enter__` on entry and `__exit__` on the way out *whatever happens*. That is `try/finally` packaged into an object. Any resource with an open/close shape is a candidate: files, sockets, locks, temporary directories, database connections.
When you expect one specific exception and want to ignore it, `contextlib.suppress` states that intent in one line:

blocks.code:
import contextlib, io

with contextlib.suppress(KeyError):
    {"a": 1}["missing"]
    print("never reached")
print("continued after the suppressed KeyError")

registry = {"web": 1, "db": 2}
for name in ["web", "cache", "db"]:
    with contextlib.suppress(KeyError):
        del registry[name]
print(registry)

blocks.text: A `suppress` block stops at the first exception inside it, so keep it to a single statement. For anything that needs a message or a fallback value, use `try/except`.

blocks.name: contextlib.suppress
blocks.sum: Ignore the named exceptions inside a with block.

how.text: It is a context manager whose `__exit__` returns true when the exception is an instance of one of the given classes, which tells Python to discard it and continue after the `with` block. Other exceptions pass through. The rest of the block after the failing line is skipped.

examples.desc: Delete a key that may not exist
examples.code:
import contextlib
d = {"x": 1}
with contextlib.suppress(KeyError):
    del d["y"]
print(d)

examples.desc: Remove a file only if it exists, from a shell one-liner
examples.code:
python3 -c 'import contextlib, pathlib
with contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError):
    pathlib.Path("scratch.tmp").unlink()
print("done")'

gotchas: Since Python 3.8 `Path.unlink(missing_ok=True)` does the same job for files; `suppress` shines for everything else.

blocks.text: Asserts: checking your own assumptions

`assert condition, message` raises `AssertionError(message)` when the condition is false. It documents an assumption that should always hold and stops the program at the first sign that your reasoning was wrong.

blocks.code:
def mask_bits(mask):
    ones = bin(mask).count("1")
    assert 0 <= ones <= 32, f"a netmask has at most 32 ones, got {ones}"
    return ones

print(mask_bits(0xFFFFFF00))
print(mask_bits(2**40 - 1))

blocks.text: The distinction to remember: **an assert checks the programmer, validation checks the user.** If a bad value can come from outside (a file, an argument, the network) raise `ValueError` or a custom error. Asserts guard conditions that can only be false if the code itself is wrong.
Running `python3 -O script.py` removes every `assert` statement. Never put work with side effects in one (`assert conn.send(data)`) and never use asserts to validate input.

blocks.name: assert
blocks.sum: Raise AssertionError when a condition is false.

how.text: The statement is roughly `if __debug__ and not condition: raise AssertionError(message)`. The message expression is only evaluated if the condition fails. `__debug__` is true unless Python runs with `-O`, which strips asserts. pytest rewrites `assert` statements in test files to show the values on both sides when they fail.

blocks.text: EAFP, LBYL and validating real data
Two styles for dealing with a risky operation:

items.text: **LBYL** ("look before you leap"): check first, then act. `if "port" in d: use(d["port"])`.
**EAFP** ("easier to ask forgiveness than permission"): act, and handle the failure. `try: use(d["port"]) except KeyError: ...`.

blocks.text: Python culture leans to EAFP, for good reasons. The check and the action in LBYL are two separate steps, and the world can change between them: another process deletes the file after `os.path.exists` said yes. Complete checks are often longer than the code they protect (try writing an `if` that tells whether `int(text)` will succeed, including `"+5"`, `" 5 "`, `"٣"`). EAFP is also usually shorter. LBYL wins when the check is cheap and the failure is common, and when you want to prevent a side effect, not just survive it.

blocks.out:
[80, 443, 22, None, 80, None, None]
[True, False, False, False, True, False, False]

blocks.text: `str.isdigit()` is False for `" 443 "` and `"+22"`, yet `int()` accepts both, and it is True for full-width digits that look odd but convert. The only reliable way to ask "will `int` accept this?" is to call `int`.
Defensive parsing of network data
Anything that arrives from a file, a socket or a command is **untrusted**: it may be truncated, in another encoding, or crafted. The pattern that scales is three layers:

items.text: A **parser function** that either returns a clean value or raises one specific exception carrying the offending text.
A **driver** that catches that exception per item, records it and carries on.
A **report** at the end that states how many items failed and shows a few.

blocks.text: The IPv6 line is rejected because of the `[ ]` brackets. The parser says exactly why it refused the line, and you can extend it deliberately instead of hoping. Note `from None` on the address error: the inner `ValueError` text from `ipaddress` would only repeat what `ParseError` already says.

items.text: Accept as little as possible, and reject with a message that contains the line number and the text.
Never `eval()` input. Use `int()`, `float()`, `json.loads`, `ipaddress` and `re`.
Decode bytes explicitly: `data.decode("utf-8", errors="replace")` keeps the program alive on invalid bytes.
Cap sizes. A socket read, a regex on a 2 GB line and a `list(range(n))` with a user-supplied `n` are all denial-of-service doors.
Return the failures to the caller (as the example does) instead of printing from inside the parser. Parsers that print cannot be reused or tested.

blocks.text: Logging instead of print

`print` is for the result of your program; **logging** is for the story of how it got there. The difference matters in a pipeline: results go to stdout where the next command reads them, diagnostics go to stderr where a human sees them. The `logging` module also gives you levels, timestamps and one switch to make a script quiet or chatty.

head: Level
Number
Use for
rows: detail you only want while hunting a bug: raw packets, every loop value
progress a user may want: "scanning 254 hosts"
something unexpected that the program handled: "line 7 skipped"

blocks.text: `logging.basicConfig()` is covered in [Python files](#py-files). The extra pieces to know here are *named loggers* and *exception logging*:

blocks.out:
DEBUG    probe: trying 192.0.2.10:22
INFO     probe: 192.0.2.10:22 open
DEBUG    probe: trying 192.0.2.10:23
WARNING  probe: 192.0.2.10:23 refused
WARNING  probe: 192.0.2.10:23 refused

blocks.text: Three habits:

items.text: **Use `%s`-style arguments, not f-strings:** `log.debug("trying %s", host)`. The text is only built if the level is enabled.
**One logger per module:** `log = logging.getLogger(__name__)`. Names appear in the output and let you tune each part of a big program separately.

**`log.exception("message")` inside an `except` block** logs at ERROR level *and appends the full traceback*. It is the right replacement for `print(e)` in a handler. `log.error("...", exc_info=True)` does the same at any level.

blocks.code:
$ python3 logdemo.py 2> errors.log; cat errors.log
2026-10-08 09:41:07,512 ERROR could not read port
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/Users/you/lab/errors/logdemo.py", line 5, in <module>
    int("http")
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'http'

blocks.text: `logging` writes to stderr by default, so `2> errors.log` captured it while any `print` output would still show on screen, exactly the stream separation from [Streams and pipes](#pipes).
The debugging loop
When something is wrong and you do not know why, work this loop instead of changing code at random:

blocks.code:
┌──▶ 1. ⟪c:Reproduce⟫     make it fail every time, with the smallest input you can
   │    2. ⟪c:Read⟫          the last traceback line and the last frame; what does it say, literally?
   │    3. ⟪c:Hypothesize⟫   write one sentence: "I think X is None because Y returned early"
   │    4. ⟪c:Observe⟫       print, log, breakpoint, or evaluate to test the sentence
   │    5. ⟪c:Fix⟫           change one thing
   └─── 6. ⟪c:Verify⟫        rerun the failing case, then the others; add a test so it stays fixed

blocks.text: Step 4 is where the tools of this chapter come in. A `print(repr(x))` is fine for a quick look (use `repr` so that `''`, `None` and `'0'` look different). When you need to look at several values, or at different moments, a debugger is faster and leaves no cleanup behind.
breakpoint() and pdb

`breakpoint()` (Python 3.7+) stops the program at that line and opens **pdb**, the standard-library debugger, in your terminal. You get a `(Pdb)` prompt at which you can inspect and step. Save this as `avg.py`:

blocks.code:
$ python3 avg.py
11.766666666666666
> /Users/you/lab/errors/avg.py(10)<module>()
-> breakpoint()
(Pdb) l
  5  	    return total / len(values)
  6
  7
  8  	readings = [11.8, 12.3, 11.2]
  9  	print(average(readings))
 10  ->	breakpoint()
 11  	print(average([]))
[EOF]
(Pdb) n
> /Users/you/lab/errors/avg.py(11)<module>()
-> print(average([]))
(Pdb) s
--Call--
> /Users/you/lab/errors/avg.py(1)average()
-> def average(values):
(Pdb) n
> /Users/you/lab/errors/avg.py(2)average()
-> total = 0
(Pdb) p values
[]
(Pdb) w
  /Users/you/lab/errors/avg.py(11)<module>()
-> print(average([]))
> /Users/you/lab/errors/avg.py(2)average()
-> total = 0
(Pdb) c
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

blocks.text: Your output will differ in details between Python versions (the arrow `->` and line numbers follow the same shape). The sequence shows the loop in action: `l` lists code, `n` runs one line, `s` steps *into* the call, `p values` prints the argument, `w` shows the stack and `c` continues to the crash.

head: Command
Long form
What it does
rows: show 11 lines of source around the current line; again for the next 11; `l .` returns to the current line
run the current line; do not enter calls on it
run the current line; enter a call if there is one
run until the current function returns
run until the next breakpoint or the end
run until line N (or until a loop finishes)
pretty-print a big dict or list
print the stack, newest frame last (marked with `>`)
move to the caller's frame / back to the callee's; `p` then works with that frame's variables
set a breakpoint on line N; `b file.py:N` or `b func` also work; `b 12, x > 3` adds a condition
run any Python statement, for example `!total = 0`; needed if a name collides with a command (a variable named `n`)
open a Python prompt with the current frame's variables

blocks.text: Pressing Enter at an empty `(Pdb)` prompt repeats the last command, so `n`, Enter, Enter, Enter walks through the code.
Two ways to enter pdb without editing the source:

items.text: `python3 -m pdb avg.py` starts the script under the debugger, stopped at the first line.

`python3 -m pdb -c continue avg.py` runs normally and drops into **post-mortem** mode when an exception ends the program, with the stack of the crash available to inspect. In a REPL after an error, `import pdb; pdb.pm()` does the same.

blocks.text: `PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 python3 avg.py` makes every `breakpoint()` a no-op, which is how you keep a forgotten one from hanging a script in cron or CI. You can also point it at another debugger, for example `PYTHONBREAKPOINT=pudb.set_trace` after `pip install pudb`.

blocks.name: breakpoint()
blocks.sum: Pause the program and open the debugger at this line.

how.text: It calls `sys.breakpointhook()`, which by default imports `pdb` and calls `pdb.set_trace()` in the caller's frame, so the prompt opens at the `breakpoint()` line itself (before Python 3.13, at the line after it). The environment variable `PYTHONBREAKPOINT` chooses another hook (`0` disables it entirely), and `sys.breakpointhook` can be reassigned in code. A breakpoint in a program that reads stdin from a pipe will fight over the terminal; run such scripts with a file argument while debugging.

examples.desc: Stop in the middle of a function when the data looks wrong
examples.code: python3 avg.py

examples.desc: Run a script with all breakpoints disabled, for example inside a pipeline
examples.code: PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 python3 avg.py | tail -n 1

gotchas: Remove debugging calls before committing; a stray `breakpoint()` hangs any non-interactive run, such as a scheduled job.

blocks.name: pdb
blocks.sum: The standard-library interactive debugger: step, inspect and change a running program.
blocks.syntax: python3 -m pdb [-c command] script.py [args]   |   import pdb; pdb.set_trace(); pdb.pm()

how.text: pdb uses the interpreter's trace hook to stop after each line when you step, or at a line number you break on. At the prompt every unknown input is evaluated as Python in the current frame, so you can print and even assign variables. `u` and `d` change the frame whose variables you see without moving execution.

Post-mortem debugging (`python3 -m pdb -c continue script.py`, or `pdb.pm()` in a REPL) examines the frame where an uncaught exception happened. The program cannot continue from there, but every variable is still alive.

flags.d: Run a pdb command at startup, for example `-c continue` to run until a crash or breakpoint.
Debug a module the way `python3 -m module` runs it.

examples.desc: Debug a script from its first line
examples.code: python3 -m pdb {{script}}

examples.desc: Run freely, then inspect the crash
examples.code: python3 -m pdb -c continue {{script}}

examples.desc: Feed scripted commands to find a value without typing (handy in a bug report)
examples.code:
printf 'b 5
c
p values
q
' | python3 -m pdb avg.py 2>&1 | grep -F '(Pdb) ['

gotchas: A variable named like a pdb command (`n`, `c`, `l`) cannot be printed by typing its name; use `p n` or `!n`.

blocks.text: The PyCharm debugger
The graphical debugger does what pdb does with a window you can see. It is the faster tool for programs with more than a few variables. The workflow:

items.text: **Set a breakpoint.** Click in the gutter (the column of line numbers) next to a line; a red dot appears. `⌘F8` toggles it on the caret line.

**Debug, not Run.** Click the bug icon next to the run button, or right-click the file and choose *Debug 'avg'*. The default macOS shortcut is `⌃D`. The program runs until it reaches the red dot and freezes **before** that line executes.

**Look at the Debug tool window.** *Threads & Variables* shows the frames (the stack) on the left and every variable in the selected frame on the right. Click a different frame to see the caller's variables, like pdb's `u`.
**Step.**

head: Action
macOS default
pdb equivalent
Meaning
rows: run this line, treat calls as one step
enter the function called on this line
finish the current function and stop in its caller
run until the line where the caret is
open a small console to compute anything in the current frame
list and edit all breakpoints, including exception breakpoints

blocks.text: The table lists PyCharm's default macOS keymap. On a laptop the F-keys may control brightness and volume unless you hold `fn`, or switch them in System Settings, Keyboard. Every action is also in the Run menu and as an icon in the Debug window, and the shortcuts are listed under Settings, Keymap if your version differs.
Power features worth knowing

items.text: **Conditional breakpoint.** Right-click the red dot and add a condition such as `port == 5432` or `len(values) == 0`. The program stops there only when the expression is true. This is how you break on the 4,000th loop pass without pressing Resume 4,000 times.

**Logging breakpoint.** Right-click the dot and choose *Evaluate and log* (or shift-click the gutter) to print an expression to the console without stopping; a `print` you can add and remove without touching the source.
**Watches.** In the variables pane click the `+` and type an expression (`len(targets)`, `host.split(".")[0]`). It is re-evaluated at every stop.
**Evaluate Expression.** Run code in the paused frame, including calls: `parse_target("cache=192.0.2.30")` to check a fix before you write it.
**Set Value.** Right-click a variable and change it; continue with the altered value to test a theory.

**Exception breakpoints.** In *View Breakpoints*, add a *Python Exception Breakpoint* for `ValueError` (or `Exception`) with *On raise*. The debugger stops at the line that raises, even when a handler would catch it later. This is the quickest way to find where a swallowed error starts.
**Run, then debug the failure.** After a crash in the Run window, the traceback lines are links to the code. Put a breakpoint above the failing line and rerun under Debug.

blocks.text: Open `probe.py` from the traceback section in PyCharm. Set a conditional breakpoint on line 13 (`name, host, port = parse_target(entry)`) with the condition `"cache" in entry`. Debug it, press Step Into (`F7`) when it stops, then step until the exception. In the variables pane read `address` and `entry`. Then use Evaluate Expression to run `address.partition(":")` and decide whether `partition` would be a better tool than `split` there.
Tests: proof that it still works

A **test** is a small program that calls your code with known inputs and fails loudly if the result differs. It converts "I ran it once and it looked right" into something you can rerun in two seconds after every change. The unit of work is a function that checks one behavior.
Start with the simplest possible test: asserts in a file. You already know `assert`.
unittest
`unittest` ships with Python (modelled on JUnit). Test cases are methods named `test_*` of a class that inherits from `unittest.TestCase`:

blocks.code:
$ python3 -m unittest -v test_portutil_unittest
test_text_is_rejected (test_portutil_unittest.ParsePortTests.test_text_is_rejected) ... ok
test_valid (test_portutil_unittest.ParsePortTests.test_valid) ... ok
test_whitespace_is_accepted (test_portutil_unittest.ParsePortTests.test_whitespace_is_accepted) ... ok
test_zero_is_rejected (test_portutil_unittest.ParsePortTests.test_zero_is_rejected) ... ok

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 4 tests in 0.000s

OK

blocks.text: The `assert*` methods (`assertEqual`, `assertTrue`, `assertIn`, `assertRaises`, `assertAlmostEqual`) exist because `unittest` could not rewrite plain asserts to show both sides. pytest can, which is the main reason most projects use it.
pytest

**pytest** is the third-party standard. Install it into your project's virtual environment (the next chapter explains why): `python3 -m pip install pytest`. Tests are plain functions named `test_*` in files named `test_*.py`, using plain `assert`:

blocks.code:
$ python3 -m pytest -q
.........                                                              [100%]
9 passed in 0.01s

blocks.text: Nine tests came from three functions: `parametrize` runs one test body once per row. When a test fails, pytest prints the values:
**Fixtures** supply set-up data to tests that name them as arguments, and tear it down afterwards. A fixture is a function decorated with `@pytest.fixture`:

Useful pytest options: `-x` stop at the first failure, `-k text` run tests whose name contains `text`, `-v` list each test, `--lf` rerun only the last failures, `--pdb` drop into pdb at a failure, `-s` show `print` output.

In a project with pytest installed, right-click `test_portutil.py` and choose *Run 'pytest in test_portutil.py'*; gutter icons appear beside each test function to run or debug a single one. A red test can be opened in the debugger like any program. If PyCharm offers *unittest*, open Settings, Tools, Python Integrated Tools, and set the default test runner to pytest.
The test-first loop
**Test-driven development** (TDD) reverses the order: write a failing test, make it pass in the simplest way, then clean up. The cycle is short (minutes) and is called red, green, refactor.

blocks.code:
⟪r:RED⟫      write a test for behavior that does not exist yet; run it; watch it fail
   ⟪g:GREEN⟫    write the least code that makes it pass; run all tests
   ⟪c:REFACTOR⟫ rename, simplify, remove duplication; run all tests again
   ──────────▶  next behavior

blocks.text: Watching the test fail first matters: it proves the test can fail. A test that never failed has not proven anything. Bugs fit this loop well too: first write a test that reproduces the bug (red), then fix it (green), and the bug cannot return unnoticed.

blocks.name: pytest
blocks.sum: Find, run and report on test functions with plain assert statements.

how.text: pytest imports files named `test_*.py` or `*_test.py`, collects functions named `test_*` and classes named `Test*`, runs each, and reports passes and failures. It rewrites the `assert` statements while importing the test module, so a failure shows the actual values of each sub-expression. Fixtures are injected by matching argument names. `python3 -m pytest` (instead of plain `pytest`) also puts the current directory on `sys.path`, which makes `from portutil import ...` work without installation.

flags.d: Quiet: one dot per test, short summary.
Run only tests whose names match the expression.
Rerun only the tests that failed last time.
Open pdb at the point of failure.
Do not capture output, so prints appear immediately.

examples.desc: Run everything quietly
examples.code: python3 -m pytest -q

examples.desc: Run one test and stop to debug it
examples.code: python3 -m pytest test_portutil.py::test_valid --pdb

examples.desc: Show only the names of failing tests, for a script or a chat message
examples.code: python3 -m pytest -q 2>&1 | grep '^FAILED'

gotchas: A test file with the same base name as another in a different folder, without `__init__.py`, collides ("import file mismatch"). Give test files unique names or add the packages.

blocks.text: Introspection: asking an object about itself

Debugging often comes down to "what is this thing?". Python can answer from inside the program. `type`, `isinstance`, `callable`, `id`, `repr` and `dir` have cards in earlier chapters; the rest are here.

blocks.code:
class Host:
    role = "unknown"
    def __init__(self, ip):
        self.ip = ip
    def ping(self):
        return f"pinging {self.ip}"

h = Host("192.0.2.5")
print(hasattr(h, "ip"), hasattr(h, "mac"))
print(getattr(h, "mac", "no mac recorded"))
setattr(h, "mac", "aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff")
print(vars(h))
delattr(h, "mac")
print(vars(h), h.role, callable(h.ping))
print(issubclass(Host, object), isinstance(h, Host))
print(hash("192.0.2.5") == hash("192.0.2." + "5"), hash((1, 2)) == hash((1, 2)))
print(repr("a\tb"), ascii("naïve"))
blocks.out:
True False
no mac recorded
{'ip': '192.0.2.5', 'mac': 'aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff'}
{'ip': '192.0.2.5'} unknown True
True True
True True
'a\tb' 'na\xefve'

blocks.name: issubclass()
blocks.sum: Tell whether one class derives from another.

how.text: True if `cls` is the same as, or inherits from, any class in `classinfo` (a class or a tuple of classes). The arguments must be classes; passing an instance raises `TypeError`. It is the class-level twin of `isinstance`, and it is what `except` effectively uses to match exception classes.

examples.desc: Check the exception tree
examples.code: print(issubclass(FileNotFoundError, OSError), issubclass(bool, int), issubclass(str, (int, float)))

examples.desc: List which built-in exceptions descend from OSError
examples.code: python3 -c 'print("\n".join(sorted(n for n, c in vars(__builtins__).items() if isinstance(c, type) and issubclass(c, OSError))))' | head -4

blocks.name: hasattr()
blocks.sum: Tell whether an object has an attribute of that name.

how.text: It calls `getattr(obj, name)` and returns False if that raises `AttributeError`. That means it also runs any property code behind the attribute. In EAFP style, writing the `try: obj.attr except AttributeError:` yourself avoids a second lookup.

examples.desc: Test for a method before calling it
examples.code: print(hasattr("text", "upper"), hasattr("text", "push"))

examples.desc: Print which of several modules provide a function, one per line
examples.code: python3 -c 'import os, sys; print(*[m.__name__ for m in (os, sys) if hasattr(m, "getpid")], sep="\n")'

blocks.name: getattr()
blocks.sum: Read an attribute by name, with an optional default.

how.text: `getattr(obj, "x")` is `obj.x` with the name held in a string, which lets you pick a method from data: `getattr(handler, "do_" + command)`. With a third argument, a missing attribute returns the default instead of raising `AttributeError`.

examples.desc: Dispatch from a string
Look up a function named in a shell variable
examples.code: fn=floor; python3 -c "import math; print(getattr(math, '$fn')(7.9))"

gotchas: Never build the attribute name from untrusted input and then call the result; it hands the caller your whole object graph.

how.text: `setattr(obj, "x", 1)` is `obj.x = 1` with a computed name. It works on instances of ordinary classes (they keep attributes in a dict), and fails on built-ins such as `str` and on classes with `__slots__` that lack the name.

examples.desc: Copy fields from a dict onto an object
examples.code:
class Config: pass
c = Config()
for k, v in {"port": 8080, "debug": True}.items():
    setattr(c, k, v)
print(c.port, c.debug)

examples.desc: Load key=value lines from a pipe into an object
examples.code:
printf 'port=80\nname=web\n' | python3 -c 'import sys
class C: pass
c = C()
for line in sys.stdin:
    k, _, v = line.strip().partition("=")
    setattr(c, k, v)
print(vars(c))'

how.text: `delattr(obj, "x")` is `del obj.x`. It raises `AttributeError` if the attribute does not exist on the instance. A class-level attribute of the same name becomes visible again afterwards.

examples.desc: Remove an instance attribute and see the class value return
examples.code:
class Host:
    role = "unknown"
h = Host(); h.role = "router"
print(h.role)
delattr(h, "role")
print(h.role)

examples.desc: Show the attribute set shrinking
examples.code:
python3 -c 'class A: pass
a = A(); a.x = 1; a.y = 2; delattr(a, "x"); print(sorted(vars(a)))'

how.text: For an ordinary object `vars(obj)` is `obj.__dict__`: the live dict that stores its attributes. Changing the dict changes the object. For a module it is the module's global names; with no argument it is `locals()`. Objects with `__slots__` or built-in types have no `__dict__` and raise `TypeError`.

examples.desc: See what an instance holds
Print a module's public names, one per line, sorted
examples.code: python3 -c 'import ipaddress; print(*sorted(n for n in vars(ipaddress) if not n.startswith("_")), sep="\n")' | head -3

blocks.name: hash()

how.text: Calls `obj.__hash__()`. Equal objects must have equal hashes, which is what lets dicts and sets find them. Mutable containers (list, dict, set) raise `TypeError: unhashable type`. String hashes are randomized per process (`PYTHONHASHSEED`), so a printed value differs on every run and must never be saved to disk or used as an ID.

examples.desc: Equal values hash equally, mutable ones cannot
Show that string hashes change between runs
examples.code: for i in 1 2; do python3 -c 'print(hash("192.0.2.1") % 1000)'; done

gotchas: For a stable fingerprint of data use `hashlib.sha256`, not `hash()`.

blocks.name: ascii()
blocks.sum: Return a printable form of an object using only ASCII characters.

how.text: Like `repr()`, but every non-ASCII character is replaced by a `\x`, `\u` or `\U` escape. It is useful for seeing what bytes arrived in a log line or hostname that contains invisible or look-alike characters (a Cyrillic "а" in a domain name looks identical to a Latin "a").

examples.desc: Reveal a look-alike character
examples.code: print(ascii("example.com"), ascii("exаmple.com"))

examples.desc: Check a hostname for non-ASCII characters
examples.code: echo 'exаmple.com' | python3 -c 'import sys; print(ascii(sys.stdin.read().strip()))'

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items.text: **Catching too much.** `except Exception: pass` hides typos like `totl` (a `NameError`). Catch the one exception you can handle meaningfully.

**Catching too early.** A low-level function that prints and returns `None` forces every caller to check. Let the exception rise to the level that knows what to do (retry, skip, show a message, exit).
**Wrapping 30 lines in one `try`.** The handler then reports the wrong cause. Wrap the one call that can raise.
**Printing the exception without its type.** `print(e)` for a `KeyError` shows `'port'`. Print `repr(e)` or use `logging.exception`.

**Using exceptions for expected flow in a hot loop.** `for` loops end with an internal `StopIteration` and that is fine, but 100 000 `KeyError`s per second is a sign that `dict.get` or `in` is the better tool.
**Debugging by editing.** If you change code before forming a hypothesis, you cannot tell which change mattered. Change one thing and rerun.
**Leaving `breakpoint()` or debug prints in committed code.**

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Parse a number or fall back

task.text: Write `safe_int(text, default=None)` that returns `int(text)`, or `default` if the text cannot be converted. It must handle both text that is not a number (`"http"`) and values that are not text at all (`None`). Do not use `isdigit`.

hints: One `try` with the conversion, and think about which two exception types `int` can raise.
`except (ValueError, TypeError):` handles both in one clause.

why.text: `int("http")` raises `ValueError` (right type, wrong content) while `int(None)` raises `TypeError` (wrong type). Catching both with a tuple handles every bad input without the bare `except` that would also hide real bugs. This one function replaces dozens of `isdigit` checks and is easier to get right.

blocks.check:
assert safe_int("443") == 443, "safe_int('443') should be 443"
assert safe_int(" 22 ") == 22, "whitespace around digits is fine for int()"
assert safe_int("http") is None, "'http' is not a number: expected None"
assert safe_int("http", -1) == -1, "the default argument should be returned"
assert safe_int(None, 0) == 0, "None raises TypeError inside int(); catch it too"

blocks.title: A custom exception with data

task.text: Define `class InvalidPort(ValueError)` whose constructor takes the offending text and stores it in the attribute `value`; its message must be `invalid port: <value!r>`. Then write `parse_port(text)` that returns an `int` from 1 to 65535 and raises `InvalidPort` for anything else (non-numeric text, or a number out of range).

hints: Call `super().__init__(message)` first so that `str(e)` returns the message, then store `self.value`.
Convert with `int()` inside try, re-raise as `InvalidPort(text)` there, and range-check afterwards.

why.text: Inheriting from `ValueError` keeps old handlers working, and the `value` attribute lets a handler report or count the bad input without parsing the message. `from None` drops the inner error because `InvalidPort` already says everything useful.

blocks.title: Retry without a decorator

task.text: Write `retry(func, attempts=3)` that calls `func()` and returns its result. If `func` raises `ConnectionError`, call it again, up to `attempts` calls in total; if the last attempt also fails, let that `ConnectionError` propagate. Any other exception must propagate immediately without a retry.

hints: A `for attempt in range(...)` loop with `try/except ConnectionError` inside it.
In the handler, re-raise with a bare `raise` when this was the last attempt; otherwise do nothing and let the loop continue.

why.text: The bare `raise` on the last attempt keeps the original traceback, so the caller sees the real failure and not your retry code. Catching only `ConnectionError` leaves bugs (`KeyError`, `TypeError`) loud. A production version would also wait between attempts, for example with `time.sleep(2 ** attempt)`.

blocks.check:
calls = []
def flaky():
    calls.append(1)
    if len(calls) < 3:
        raise ConnectionError("refused")
    return "ok"
assert retry(flaky) == "ok", "should succeed on the third call"
assert len(calls) == 3, f"expected 3 calls, got {len(calls)}"
n = []
def dead():
    n.append(1)
    raise ConnectionError("down")
try:
    retry(dead, attempts=2)
    raise AssertionError("should have re-raised ConnectionError")
except ConnectionError:
    pass
assert len(n) == 2, f"expected exactly 2 attempts, got {len(n)}"
m = []
def buggy():
    m.append(1)
    raise KeyError("x")
try:
    retry(buggy)
    raise AssertionError("KeyError should propagate")
except KeyError:
    pass
assert len(m) == 1, "a KeyError must not be retried"

blocks.title: Fix the crash from its traceback

task.text: This function crashes on the third entry with `ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 2, got 1)`. Fix `load_targets` so that it returns a dict mapping name to `(host, port)` for the valid entries and **skips** entries without a colon. Keep the order of entries. A valid entry looks like `web=192.0.2.10:443`.

hints: Both the unpack failure and `int("http")` raise `ValueError`, so one `except ValueError` covers all malformed entries.
Put the `try` inside the loop so that a bad entry only skips itself.

why.text: A `try` placed outside the loop would stop the whole load at the first bad entry. Inside the loop, each entry is handled on its own. The better production version records the skipped entries so they can be reported, as in the parsing section.

blocks.check:
data = ["web=192.0.2.10:443", "db=192.0.2.20:5432", "cache=192.0.2.30"]
assert load_targets(data) == {"web": ("192.0.2.10", 443), "db": ("192.0.2.20", 5432)}, "valid entries only"
assert load_targets([]) == {}
assert list(load_targets(["b=198.51.100.1:1", "a=198.51.100.2:2"])) == ["b", "a"], "keep order"
assert load_targets(["x=192.0.2.1:http"]) == {}, "a non-numeric port should also be skipped"

blocks.title: Crash it, read it, step through it

task.text: Save `probe.py` from the traceback section into `~/lab/errors/`. Part 1: run it and write down, from the traceback alone, the line number where Python gave up and the line number of the call that supplied the bad data. Part 2: run `python3 -m pdb -c continue probe.py`. After the crash, use `p entry`, `p address`, `u`, `p entry` and `w` to confirm your answer. Part 3: fix `parse_target` by raising a `ValueError("bad entry: ...")` with the offending text before the unpack, and prove the new message shows the entry.

hints: In post-mortem mode the prompt shows the frame of the crash. `u` moves to the caller where `entry` is also visible.
`if ":" not in address: raise ValueError(f"missing port in entry {entry!r}")`
blocks.solution:
python3 probe.py
python3 -m pdb -c continue probe.py

why.text: The deepest frame shows where the unpack failed, and the frame above it shows which `entry` led there. A message that contains the data (`'cache=192.0.2.30'`) lets you find the problem from the last line of the traceback without a debugger.

blocks.title: Which exception?

task.text: For each statement, name the exception Python raises and say whether it is more likely a bug in the code or bad input: (1) `ports = [22, 80]; ports[2]` (2) `int("22/tcp")` (3) `{"ip": "192.0.2.1"}["host"]` (4) `len(5)` (5) `"192.0.2.1".split(".")[4]` (6) `open("/etc/hostz")`.

blocks.solution: 1. IndexError. A bug, or a loop bound that is off by one. 2. ValueError. Bad input. 3. KeyError. Bad input if the dict is from a file, a bug if you built it. 4. TypeError. A bug. 5. IndexError. Bad input if the string came from outside, since it has only four parts. 6. FileNotFoundError. Environment or input, depending on where the path came from.

why.text: Telling bugs from bad input decides what to do next. Bugs should crash loudly while you are developing; bad input must be anticipated, handled and reported.

questions.q: In a traceback, which line should you read first?

options.text: The first line, "Traceback (most recent call last)"
The top frame, because it is the oldest
The last line, which names the exception type and message
The file name in the first frame

questions.why: The exception type and message are printed last. The frame just above it is where the error was detected, and the frames above that show the chain of calls that led there.

questions.q: What does this print? ```python def f(): try: return "try" finally: print("cleanup") print(f()) ```
questions.why: `finally` runs after the return value is computed but before the function returns, so "cleanup" prints first, then the caller prints the result.
`FileNotFoundError` is a subclass of `OSError`, as are `PermissionError`, `TimeoutError` and `ConnectionError`.

questions.q: What is the difference between `raise` and `raise X from err` inside an except clause?

options.text: `raise` creates a new exception, `from` re-raises the old one
A bare `raise` re-raises the current exception unchanged; `raise X from err` raises a new exception and records `err` as its cause
There is none, they print the same traceback

questions.why: Bare `raise` keeps the exception and its traceback. `from err` sets `__cause__`, and the printed traceback says the first error was the direct cause of the second.

questions.q: Which pdb command runs the current line and enters the function it calls?
questions.why: `s` (step) enters calls; `n` (next) runs the line without entering them; `r` runs until the current function returns.

questions.q: Why is `assert port > 0` the wrong way to validate a port number typed by a user?

options.text: Asserts are slower than if statements
Asserts are removed with `python3 -O`, and they are meant for programmer assumptions, not input checks

questions.why: Run with `-O`, every assert disappears, so the check would silently vanish. Validate input with an explicit `if` and raise `ValueError` or a custom exception.

blocks.text: Project: netparse, a ping-log parser with tests

blocks.title: netparse.py, a tested parser for ping output

blocks.text: The saved `~/lab/ping.log` is the output of `ping -c 10 example.com` on macOS: a header, ten lines with a time per reply (one is a timeout), then a statistics block. You will write a parser that turns it into numbers, rejects damaged lines with a clear error, and has tests that prove both. This module feeds the `latency-log` idea from the networking part and the `netkit` capstone.
Step 1: The parser

The line formats are `64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=0 ttl=56 time=11.842 ms` and `Request timeout for icmp_seq 5`. Everything else (header, blank, `--- example.com ping statistics ---`, the packet summary) is recognised or ignored on purpose. Save as `netparse.py`:

The structure follows the rules from the defensive-parsing section: `parse_line` raises one specific error that carries the line number and text, `parse_ping` catches it per line and collects it, and nothing is printed from inside the parser (the `log.warning` goes to the logging system, which the caller can silence or route).
Step 2: Tests
Install pytest in an environment first (the next chapter explains it; for now `python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && pip install pytest`). Save as `test_netparse.py`:

blocks.code:
import pytest
from netparse import PingParseError, parse_line, parse_ping

GOOD = """PING example.com (93.184.216.34): 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=0 ttl=56 time=11.842 ms
Request timeout for icmp_seq 1
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=2 ttl=56 time=12.310 ms

--- example.com ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 33.3% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 11.842/12.076/12.310/0.234 ms
"""


def test_reply_line():
    assert parse_line(1, "64 bytes from 192.0.2.1: icmp_seq=4 ttl=64 time=0.5 ms") == ("reply", 4, 0.5)


def test_timeout_line():
    assert parse_line(1, "Request timeout for icmp_seq 7") == ("timeout", 7, None)


def test_header_is_ignored():
    assert parse_line(1, "PING example.com (93.184.216.34): 56 data bytes") is None


@pytest.mark.parametrize("bad", ["garbage", "64 bytes from x: icmp_seq=1 ttl=5 time=1 ms", "64 bytes from 192.0.2.1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=5 time=0.0 ms"])
def test_bad_lines_raise(bad):
    with pytest.raises(PingParseError) as info:
        parse_line(9, bad)
    assert info.value.lineno == 9


def test_whole_run():
    r = parse_ping(GOOD)
    assert r["rtts"] == [11.842, 12.310]
    assert r["lost"] == 1
    assert r["summary"] == (3, 2)
    assert r["errors"] == []


def test_damaged_input_is_reported_not_fatal():
    r = parse_ping(GOOD + "this line is damaged\n")
    assert len(r["errors"]) == 1
    assert r["rtts"] == [11.842, 12.310]

python3 -m pytest -q
python3 -c 'from netparse import parse_ping; r = parse_ping(open("ping.log").read()); print(len(r["rtts"]), "replies,", r["lost"], "lost")'

blocks.text: The second command, run in `~/lab`, should print `9 replies, 1 lost`, which matches the `10 packets transmitted, 9 packets received` line in the log.
Step 3: Break it, debug it

items.text: Append `garbage` to a copy of `ping.log` and run the parser. The error list should contain one `PingParseError` with the right line number.
Change a regular expression slightly (for example drop the `ttl=` part) so tests fail. Read the pytest failure, then rerun with `python3 -m pytest -x --pdb` and inspect `line` and `m` at the failure.
Add a test first for a new behavior (an `Request timeout` line with no number must be an error), watch it fail, then make it pass.

blocks.text: Add `stats(rtts)` returning min, mean, max and the mean absolute difference between consecutive RTTs (jitter). Add a `--file` option with `argparse` once you have read the next chapter. Compare your `lost` count to the packet-loss percentage in the summary and report a mismatch as an error.
Next: [Modules, packages and the command line](#py-modules) takes your scripts and turns them into importable modules, isolated environments and real command-line tools with `argparse`.

terms.def: The report Python prints for an uncaught exception, listing the active calls from oldest to newest and ending with the exception type and message
An object that signals a failure and travels up the call stack until a handler catches it
Leaving function calls one by one, looking for a matching except clause, after an exception is raised
The except clause (or the code in it) that deals with an exception
Easier to ask forgiveness than permission: try the operation and handle the failure
Look before you leap: check conditions first, then act
An exception that records another as its cause or context, so the traceback shows both
A marked line at which the debugger pauses the program
Inspecting the stack of a program after it crashed with an uncaught exception
Reusable setup code that pytest passes into tests by argument name
A pytest feature that runs one test function with many sets of arguments
Test-driven development: write a failing test, make it pass, refactor, repeat
A named logging channel that applies levels and handlers to the messages sent to it
